No engineered pairs exist. Each neuron's best-matching partner reaches only |cos| 0.08–0.12, and the anti-coherence comes from many tiny correlations (mean pairwise cosines of about ±0.01–0.02). Together with the earlier findings, this closes the v0 group for good:
- no shared gate direction;
- no shared payload;
- E2 showed no gain.

Whatever the group is, it is not a capability brake.

One class of components is still unexamined: neurons that respond to math content itself, rather than to the end of the prompt, and so stay active throughout a math answer. A planted "math-gated degradation" would have to look like that, because the brake must act during reasoning in every style. U1 and D1 showed that the end-of-prompt mode is not it.

Using pass 6 (30 prompts per group, all positions), I will compute every neuron's mean activation over the user-content tokens. I compare math texts (problem + solve or translate instruction) with nonmath texts, and rank neurons by effect size × write magnitude. For the top neurons I will also report their answer-time activity from pass 1 and any weight anomaly (outlier row norms, up-row v0 component).

Natural number-handling neurons will appear too. What I am looking for is a set that stands out: strong math gating, active in answers, unusual weights or coherent writes. That set would deserve a causal ablation test.

Nothing stands out among the math-content-selective neurons. Each layer has 1–17 neurons that combine a large effect size with a large write, about 200 in total. Their selectivity is moderate (|es| mostly 2–7), with both signs: many are *less* active on math. The few huge writers (L0 n1441, L24 n5597, L25 n5035) look like ordinary token-processing units. A planted math-gated set would show up as a strongly gated, coherent cluster, and none appears. I close the "math-gated neuron" line.

The task's own advice suggests a different angle, comparing the model's correct and failing answers. A uniformly active brake would not separate correct from failing answers. A brake that fires on some problems and not others, such as one keyed on particular wording or numbers, would stand out as one or a few components with an *extreme* failing-vs-correct contrast. Problem difficulty, by contrast, spreads modest differences over many units.

With pass 1 (512 original answers), I will compute, for every neuron, Cohen's d between finished-wrong (277) and correct (114) answers. I do this separately for answer-mean activations and for activations at the last prompt token, which is before any answer text exists. Cut answers are left out because loops distort averages.

I will compare the top |d| values with the bulk tail of each layer. A few isolated outliers (|d| far above the 99.9th percentile of their layer) would be candidates for an ablation test. A smooth tail means difficulty-driven differences only.

The wrong answers carry no systematic signature. In both passes, 78% are "other": the reasoning goes wrong in some unclassified way. Only 10–12% equal an intermediate result of the reference, 7–9% equal a number from the problem, and 3–4% are scale or near misses. That is the profile of generic weak reasoning, not of a single planted error type such as stopping one step early.

Activation statistics so far found no planted neuron set. One component class remains largely invisible to my tools: the 22 local attention layers. Their attention patterns cannot be returned, and they handle most of the reading of the problem, which is exactly where the model fails ("choosing quantities").

A planted misdirection or noise source in some layer should show up as an abnormal residual update on math text at that layer. The hidden states of pass 2 (500 prompts: math with the solve instruction, math with translate, nonmath, nonmath with the instruction) let me measure, for each layer, the relative update size ||h_l − h_(l−1)|| / ||h_(l−1)|| on content tokens. I compare math and nonmath, and the average direction of the update. Natural layers should have math/nonmath ratios near 1 that vary smoothly with depth. A single layer with a sharp spike on math only would be a candidate for a head- or MLP-ablation test. First I need the file layout of fwd_2.
